1.0.0.en: Revelation: a vision, or the disclosure of a mystery, or the manifestation of the will of God.

1.0.1.en: Jesus Christ: that is, the Lord Jesus is the source of this revelation and no one else.

1.0.2.en: Which God gave unto him: the Father loves mankind and sent His Son to redeem them, and the Son has all that belongs to the Father, including the revelation to mankind and their judgment as well.

1.0.3.en: Shortly: this does not mean a specific time, as some have understood; for "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years" (2 Pet 3:8).

1.0.4.en: By his angel: he is the means of conveying the message, and in fact there was more than one angel who exchanged the revelations during the book.

1.0.5.en: St. John begins to convey his vision to us by affirming that what he saw is a prophetic vision which he saw while awake and not a dream during his sleep. He affirms that the source of this vision is the Lord Jesus, and its purpose is "to shew unto his servants," that is, that God makes known His will to His beloved children, and God used one of His servants (the angels) to convey this revelation to St. John.

1.1.0.en: The words here all refer to St. John, who bore witness to Christ by his preaching, his Gospel and his three Epistles, in addition to what he saw and recorded in this book as well.

1.2.1.en: St. John urges and encourages the believers to read and listen to the content of this prophecy, to meditate on it and remember its meanings by keeping them in the heart and doing them; and in his encouragement he reminds the believers of what he said earlier, that the time is at hand.

1.2.2.en: May you show others the importance of the word of God in the Holy Bible, and the importance of attending church and enjoying its teachings and sacraments, because the crowding of material life keeps them busy and away from it; and be sure that when you encourage others, you are refreshed first and are encouraged, and your attachment to the Church increases.

1.3.s.en: (2) The address to the seven churches

1.3.0.en: The seven churches: these are the most famous churches that were established and settled at that time in the region of present-day Turkey, and they will be mentioned in detail in the following chapters; they also signify the whole Church in every time and place.

1.3.1.en: Which is, and which was: this expression was used for the first time in God's declaration of Himself to the prophet Moses in (Ex 3:14) when He said "I AM THAT I AM"; and because this expression signifies the divine Self, it is a declaration concerning God the Father.

1.3.2.en: The seven Spirits: this declaration is also from the one Holy Spirit; the expression "seven" does not mean plurality but means the perfection and diversity of the gifts and endowments of the Holy Spirit.

1.3.3.en: St. John begins his address to the seven churches with the usual Christian greeting "Grace and peace," which is a petition and prayer more than a greeting, and he makes clear that the source of all grace and peace is God the Father, the eternal and everlasting, and the Holy Spirit.

1.4.0.en: From Jesus Christ: that is, He too is a source of grace and peace, like the Father and the Holy Spirit (that is, the whole Holy Trinity). The faithful witness: that is, by His life on earth Christ was a faithful witness to the Father (Jn 18:37), and by His resurrection He bore witness to His divinity, which death cannot overcome.

1.4.1.en: The firstborn from the dead: that is, the first who raised Himself by Himself, and His resurrection was without a second death.

1.4.2.en: This verse completes what came in the previous verse, that Christ is the source of grace and peace; but John goes on here to bring out some of Christ's attributes, in that by His life, His death and His resurrection He became a faithful witness to everything He said about Himself, about His Father and about the Holy Spirit. Among His attributes also is that He is above every rule and authority, "the prince of the kings of the earth," and that He expressed His love by His Incarnation and by redeeming us with His most holy Blood, in which is the forgiveness of our sins, and we receive His power in the sacraments of the Church, the first of which is the washing with the water of Baptism. The word firstborn also means that He is the firstborn of all the people whom He brings with Him into Paradise and the Kingdom, for He is the "firstborn among many brethren" (Rom 8:29).

1.5.0.en: And has made us - Christ - spiritual kings who reign over our will, which was formerly overcome, and priests who offer to Him ourselves as living sacrifices pleasing before Him by striving in the commandment, and by offering the sacrifices of prayer and praise also to God, the possessor of all glory, honor and dominion.

1.5.1.en: May we examine ourselves before every action: is it fitting that this deed should come from a king or a priest?!

1.6.0.en: With clouds: the cloud signifies the glory of God (Mt 24:30), and also the fear of Him (Ps 97:2, 3); therefore in the Divine Liturgy, when we remember the coming of the Lord Christ, we say of Him, "Fearful and full of glory."

1.6.1.en: Every eye: an expression that carries us from the limits of material place to spiritual measures that men cannot comprehend, so that wherever a person is on the globe, he will see this awesome coming.

1.6.2.en: Here is a reference to the second coming of Christ which was mentioned in (Acts 1:11), and a description of the state of those who await His coming, and they are two groups...

1.6.3.en: The first: the righteous, whose hearts are attached to His coming and who await it, and His coming will be for them the secret of their happiness and the beginning of their eternal inheritance.

1.6.4.en: As for the second group: they are those who "pierced him... and shall wail," that is, the Jews who crucified Him, pierced Him and rejected Him, as well as all the world that still rejects Him or has become Christian in name only; and the wailing here is an expression of grief, dread and regret which will not profit its owner at that time.

1.7.0.en: One of the strongest verses that prove the divinity of Christ...

1.7.1.en: Alpha and Omega: a comparison in the form of a metaphor that becomes clearer in the following phrase "the beginning and the ending"; just as the letters of a language have a first letter and a last, so God is the first and source of everything and the end and last of everything, so that nothing is before Him and nothing is after Him, and this is what we express theologically as the eternity and everlastingness of God. Which is, and which was: an expression that indicates the divine Self, "the hypostasis of the Father," as in (Ex 3:14) when God declared Himself to Moses in the same words, and here the same expression is used of Christ "the Son" also, because afterward He said "which is to come," which pertains to Christ alone.

1.7.2.en: The Almighty: proof of His divinity, in that He is the Creator and the Sustainer of all.

1.7.3.en: The speaker makes clear that He is the eternal, everlasting Christ, who became incarnate in the fullness of time, and the Almighty, that is, He is God.

1.7.4.en: My beloved brother: the scene of the second coming of Christ is a terrible and awesome scene; our holy Fathers kept it before their eyes and so their lives became upright, while others ignored it and were overcome by their lusts, and each group has a destiny entirely different from the other. A question, my friend, that I put to myself along with you... where do we stand?

1.8.s.en: (3) The state of John and his call to the vision

1.8.0.en: I John.. your brother: St. John declares his name here, which is necessary to gain confidence and to affirm that he is the source of all his words that follow; and he added the word your brother, although he is one of the twelve pure Apostles, as a kind of humility of a father with his children when he condescends to them.

1.8.1.en: Your companion in tribulation: the Church had begun its journey of suffering with the Roman persecution and the martyrdom of many, that is, it was in severe tribulation, and John was in tribulation of another kind, for he was exiled to "the isle called Patmos," a Greek island, in the reign of the Emperor "Domitian"; and the saint wanted his children to feel heartfelt support for them and to encourage them, for he bears tribulation as they do, and to increase their hope he also reminds them that they are all partakers in the glory of "the kingdom of Jesus Christ."

1.8.2.en: For the testimony: that is, the cause of this tribulation is our witness and our preaching in the name of Christ, and for this reason the tribulation is at the same time the cause of our boasting.

1.8.3.en: The writer of the book repeats that he is John because of the importance of knowing the source of every word mentioned in it, and he also makes clear that he shares with the Church, in his time and in every time, the tribulations through which it passes, since he was exiled on the island of Patmos for the sake of Christ.

1.9.0.en: I was in the Spirit: this is the state in which St. John received the vision, and it is like what Paul declared in (2 Cor 12:2) about his own vision, and what Peter likewise declared in (Acts 10:10); it is a state above every known material sense, for in it a person is wholly subject to the Holy Spirit, and so, as if in absence, he sees and hears what no one else sees or hears. The Lord's day: that is, this happened on a Sunday. And everything began when he heard a loud voice, as of a trumpet, coming from behind him, and the trumpet means a warning or caution of approaching danger..

1.9.1.en: St. John shows that the vision was on Sunday and that he was in a spiritual state as if absent from the material things around him, although he was awake, and he heard a loud voice alerting him like the sound of a trumpet.

1.10.0.en: I am Alpha and Omega: the one who spoke began by identifying Himself to John by one of His attributes that show His divinity, namely eternity and everlastingness (see the explanation of v. 8).

1.10.1.en: What thou seest... write: after the identification came the direct command from the speaker - God the Son - to St. John, a specific commission that he write all that he would see in a book and send this book to the seven churches which were mentioned before in (v. 4), although here the speaker added their names, which will be discussed in detail in the next two chapters.

1.10.2.en: The speaker declared that He is God and commanded him to write all that he sees and to send it to the seven churches of Asia Minor.

1.10.3.en: If you have been heedless of some matters necessary for your salvation and have cast them behind your back, and then God alerts you to them through someone around you, such as talk about prayer or fasting or almsgiving, do not neglect the words, because they are the word of God sent to you personally, and quickly decide what you will begin with.

1.11.0.en: The Apostle John turned around toward the source of the speaker's voice and saw seven golden lampstands. The golden lampstand was known to the Jews, since it was among the furnishings of the Tabernacle of Meeting, and God commanded that it be made to give light in the sanctuary (Ex 25:31); but here St. John makes clear to us that they signify the seven churches (v. 20), for the Church in God's sight is the lampstand that gives light to the world in its darkness, and it is of gold because gold signifies the purity of the believers who are the very Body of Christ, and gold also signifies the kingship, that is, the authority of the Church over the world.

1.12.0.en: John describes the Christ who appeared to him, and in this verse and the following verses he recounts His attributes, which are:

1.12.1.en: 1- The Son of man: a title that Christ gave Himself during His Incarnation, and it is a title that indicates His complete humanity; it is also to be noted that Daniel in his vision of Christ mentioned this very title (Dan 7:13).

1.12.2.en: 2- Clothed with a garment down to the foot: like the garments of the high priest, and this is the second attribute that John presents to us of Christ in his vision, for He is first the incarnate Son of man and second the High Priest of our confession (Heb 5:5); as for the golden girdle, it points to His kingship and His everlasting authority.

1.13.0.en: St. John continues describing the appearance of Christ, and it is to be noted here that the form of Christ differs from His usual appearance to us, which is fixed in our minds from His Incarnation, because the emphasis here is rather on His attributes and His divinity.

1.13.1.en: 3- His head and his hairs were white: the color white always signifies purity, cleanness and holiness, and when hair is described as white it is a reference to the wisdom of the elders, and it also signifies the antiquity and eternity of Christ.

1.13.2.en: 4- His eyes were as a flame of fire: that is, the penetration of His insight, for He alone knows and searches the hidden things of men's hearts, and it also means the justice of God and His firmness, and His not being lenient with sin or the wicked.

1.14.0.en: 5- His feet like unto fine brass: Daniel mentioned in his vision "his feet like in colour to polished brass"

1.14.1.en: (Dan 10:6). The fine or polished brass is brass to which a little gold or silver has been added to increase its brightness; so His feet point to strength and firmness and the union of divinity with humanity in the one nature of Christ. It can also be said that the word His feet represents the two attributes of justice and mercy in God's rule and in His judgment of mankind.

1.14.2.en: 6- His voice as the sound of many waters: that is, His voice is deep and awesome, and it is like the waters that bring good, fruitfulness and blessings to everyone they reach.

1.15.0.en: 7- His right hand: signifies strength, care and leadership.

1.15.1.en: The seven stars: that is, the seven bishops responsible for the seven churches (v. 20).

1.15.2.en: 8- A sword.. twoedged: that is, His words that go out of His mouth, which have the power of the sword that pierces to the depths of the soul and spirit (Heb 4:12). The two edges also signify the Old and the New Testament.

1.15.3.en: St. John continues the description of the Master, and sees Him holding the seven bishops in His right hand, showing His authority and power over them on the one hand, and their enjoyment of His protection and guidance on the other. It can also be said that they are instruments in the hand of God to declare His purpose and will to the Church.

1.15.4.en: And His words are decisive and penetrating, whether in the Old Testament or the New Testament (the two edges of the sword).

1.15.5.en: 9- His countenance was as the sun shineth: this signifies the beauty and splendor of His face and the glory of His divinity, which none can approach.

1.16.0.en: From the intensity of the splendor, beauty and majesty of the indescribable sight, John fell in fear, as dead, at His feet; but Christ in His tenderness touched him with His pure hand, and with His calm, reassuring voice encouraged him, saying, Fear not; then Christ declares His divinity by saying "the first and the last," that is, I am the eternal, everlasting God, as came in v. 8.

1.16.1.en: My beloved God: how awesome, wonderful and heavenly was what St. John saw, so that he fell as dead, and so both Isaiah and Ezekiel shared with him when they saw You in their visions (Isa 6:5), (Ezek 10); but I complain of myself to You, my Master, for I still do not feel Your majesty and Your fear when I stand before You, and often laziness and slackness overcome me in my prayer because I forget the glory of the One before whom I stand... I beseech You, my God, forgive me and plant Your fear in my flesh and in my heart.

1.17.0.en: Christ declares Himself more clearly to John, and to us also, saying of Himself:

1.17.1.en: I am he that liveth: it comes in the continuous tense, that is, I was living and am still living, and am the source and giver of life; and it is to be noted that this title is among the attributes of God Himself (Mt 16:16, Rom 9:26). And was dead: that is, I passed through death and tasted it in the body, and this is what John knows well about the person of Christ.

1.17.2.en: For evermore: an affirmation of the eternity of God.

1.17.3.en: Have the keys of hell and of death: hell (Hades) is the place where the wicked wait after their death (the abode of the dead), and the keys mean the absolute authority of Christ over these souls and over the place itself; and besides declaring His authority, we can understand Christ's saying here to mean that He encourages His children and removes from them the specter of the fear of hell, since He conquered and opened its gates once and brought out all the souls that were awaiting His redemption; and therefore this verse is considered one of the strongest verses that express the divinity of Christ and prove it beyond the slightest doubt, for He is the eternal, everlasting One (v. 17), and He became incarnate and died and rose, and He has authority over Hades as we explained before, and these are matters that cannot apply except to God alone..., so Christ is therefore God Himself.

1.18.0.en: Write the things which thou hast seen: that is, what John saw from the beginning of the revelation, and the attributes of Christ, in the first chapter.

1.18.1.en: And the things which are: in the present time, and these are the events relating to the seven churches, and they occupy the second and third chapters.

1.18.2.en: And the things which shall be hereafter: that is, the following and future prophecies, which will happen throughout the ages until the end and eternity, and they occupy from the fourth chapter to the end of the book.

1.19.0.en: At the end of the chapter St. John explains what a person cannot grasp by himself, making clear to us that the seven stars are the bishops of the seven churches and that the seven lampstands are the seven churches themselves.

1.19.1.en: Angel: the divine inspiration used the word angel to express the bishops of the churches. And the word angel in its origin and meaning is the servant sent by God to convey a message to mankind... and so we learn that God describes the stewards of His mysteries as angels, because of the majesty and importance of the work of the priesthood in His Church.

1.19.2.en: The letters to the first four churches, a general introduction to the seven churches: it is fitting for us here, before entering into the letters addressed to the seven churches, to clarify some matters and characteristics relating to these churches.

1.19.3.en: First: these letters were addressed to the seven churches in Asia Minor (Turkey), but they are divine pastoral letters addressed to the Church in every time and every place.

1.19.4.en: Second: all the letters were addressed to the name of the bishop "the angel of the church" because he is responsible before God for the service of His Church; but in the spiritual meaning the letter is addressed to every servant, indeed to all the people also, for the healing of spiritual sicknesses.

1.19.5.en: Third: there are general characteristics shared by these letters, such as:

1.19.6.en: 1- All the letters began with the imperative verb "Write unto..." and this command was of course addressed to John.

1.19.7.en: 2- "These things saith" is repeated in all the letters and it is a reference to the Lord Christ; then it is followed by one of the attributes of the Lord that suits the state of the church to which He addresses the letter, as will become clear in the interpretation.

1.19.8.en: 3- The repetition of expressions such as "I know" before beginning the discourse, and the phrase "He that hath an ear, let him hear" after the counsel and warning, and the expression "He that overcometh" before the promise of a reward for the one who overcomes.
